revisions.body: Before any speech begins, the dialogue makes us notice its route of transmission. The unnamed companion asks Apollodorus, who heard the banquet from Aristodemus; Apollodorus says he checked some details with Socrates. The account is told while they walk to Athens. That layered, moving frame ensures that we hear the speeches as reported memory, not as direct access to the feast.

Apollodorus presents philosophy as a change in his scale of value. Before following Socrates daily, he says, he ran about aimlessly while thinking he was accomplishing something; philosophical talk now gives him immense pleasure, while talk from the wealthy and money-makers irritates him. Before he reports the banquet, then, he has already declared which kinds of speech he can hear as meaningful.

Agathon makes physical contact the imagined medium of instruction: sit beside me, he says, and I may gain the wisdom that came to you. Socrates answers with a conditional image of wisdom flowing from the fuller to the emptier through wool. The scene turns bodily proximity into a question: can wisdom actually be transferred by nearness?

Before anyone praises Eros, the gathering negotiates what kind of gathering it will be. The guests settle for moderate drinking; Eryximachus replaces the flute-girl’s entertainment with speeches, supplies the topic, and sets the order, while Socrates notes that the arrangement is unequal for those reclining last. The point is not the inventory: the contest is made through consent, and its rules remain visible.

Read this opening beside Theaetetus 142a–143c. The comparison is useful not as a generic paper-versus-memory contrast, but as a question about verification: here Apollodorus identifies Aristodemus as his source and says he checked some details with Socrates. What matters is that the dialogue makes the route of transmission part of what we hear.

crossrefs.note: the Theaetetus frame delivers a written, Socrates-checked transcript, in contrast with the Symposium's oral transmission chain

revisions.body: Here Phaedrus turns three myths into a scale of erotic sacrifice. Alcestis establishes the admirable case: she dies for her husband and receives restoration. Orpheus supplies the failure: he seeks the beloved without accepting death. Achilles becomes the highest case, choosing Patroclus even after learning that this choice will cost him his own life. The sequence makes Phaedrus’s standard visible: divine honor rises with the lover’s willingness to risk, and finally surrender, his life for the beloved.
Phaedrus now scales an intimate bond into a city or army. Does that move reveal a political theory of virtue, or does it merely enlarge the audience before whom erotic honor must be maintained?

Pausanias turns the encomium into a classification exercise. He objects that the group was told simply to praise Eros, then announces that he will first identify which Eros deserves praise and only afterward praise him. The move does not prove that his framework has won the contest; it shows how he makes his own definition the condition for proceeding.

Pausanias proposes that a law should forbid loving boys because their eventual character is uncertain. He then says good men voluntarily impose that rule on themselves, while popular lovers ought to be compelled to follow it. The sharp point is not that he reports no law exists; rather, his wording shifts between an ideal rule and the pressure he thinks should enforce it.

Pausanias lets Athens appear to say two opposite things. Lovers are publicly indulged, yet fathers and companions publicly restrain the beloved. His resolution is that neither side settles the matter by itself: the act becomes noble or shameful according to how it is conducted.

At 181a, Pausanias makes a condition, not an essence, govern praise: drinking, singing, speaking, and loving become noble or base according to how they are done. This is the hinge of his distinction: the subject is not love in the abstract, but the manner in which an erotic impulse directs action.

revisions.title: Eryximachus: Eros in the whole of nature
revisions.body: Eryximachus widens Pausanias's twofold Eros from human relations to bodies, music, and the seasons. His craft does not simply reject the popular love: both kinds remain present and must be guarded, while the orderly love should govern their use. The doctor thus turns a distinction into a program of management.

The hiccup turns a speech schedule into a medical exchange. Aristophanes asks Eryximachus either to cure him or speak in his place; the doctor accepts both roles and escalates from breath-holding to gargling to induced sneezing. The bodily event therefore does more than interrupt the scene: it hands one speaker's turn to another and makes medicine manage the conversation itself.

Listen for how medicine is recast as erotic expertise. Eryximachus defines it as knowledge of bodily loves in repletion and depletion, then gives the practitioner four tasks: distinguish the better and worse love, transform one into another, implant love where it should exist, and remove it where it should not. Reconciliation of opposites is one culmination, not the whole job.

Notice the force of Eryximachus's correction. He says perhaps Heraclitus wished to say the right thing: harmony arises when high and low notes, formerly at variance, later agree through musical art. He also calls the wording ill-spoken and argues that harmony cannot consist in things still disagreeing. One way to hear the moment is as a speaker's revision of a quoted thinker, not as a neutral report.

Eryximachus has made the vocabulary of love reach across medicine, music, and other human and divine affairs. At the close, he distinguishes Love as a whole from the form completed with moderation and justice, then admits that he may have omitted much and hands Aristophanes the task of filling the gaps. If this praise also displays the speaker's method, what exactly is being praised?

Aristophanes now names the force his myth has been describing. Eros is innate in human beings, a gatherer of their ancient nature, trying to make one from two and heal the human condition. After Hephaestus offers to fuse the lovers, Aristophanes gives the reason: we were once whole, so the desire and pursuit of the whole is called eros. The definition makes longing intelligible as a search for lost unity.

revisions.title: From praise's rule to Eros's portrait
revisions.body: This unit follows Agathon's method from rule to performance: praise should first say what Eros is, then what he causes. The resulting portrait makes him youngest, softest, and fluid in form, using poetic analogy and functional reasoning; the closing self-describes the speech as a mixture of play and measured seriousness.

At 196c, Agathon's praise of temperance is a compressed inference: if temperance means mastering pleasures and Eros is stronger than every pleasure, then Eros masters them. The conclusion depends on that ranking; hear the argument as a logical hinge, not merely another item in the virtue catalogue.

At the close, Agathon describes his speech as a mixture of play and measured seriousness. What changes in how you hear the catalogue that has just ended? Does the formula settle its tone, or leave you to weigh the two modes?

At 201c, the pressure comes from carrying Agathon’s own agreements one step farther. Once he has accepted that Eros lacks beauty, Socrates adds the premise that good things are beautiful and draws the parallel conclusion that Eros lacks good things. Agathon answers that he cannot contradict Socrates. What matters here, I think, is the form of the refutation: the conclusion has been assembled from assent rather than announced as a fresh description.
For a forward comparison, carry this distinction to 200d–200e: desire will be recast as wanting present goods to remain present in the future, not simply as possessing what one already has.

crossrefs.note: Socrates distinguishes present possession from wanting continued possession in future time.

revisions.body: The argument stalls at a precise point: Socrates can say what the lover wants—beautiful things to be his—but not what possession would yield. Diotima then changes the term under discussion, asking the same question about good things; Socrates can answer, “happiness.” The move gets the exchange forward, but the passage leaves its justification open.

Diotima briefly takes up a story about lovers seeking their other half, then gives it a condition: love is neither for half nor whole unless that object is good. The point is not to debate the story at length. The scene shifts attention from belonging as such to the good that a person can call his own.

In the Republic, the philosopher desires the whole of wisdom; here, Eros is placed between wisdom and ignorance. The shared title does not erase the difference: Diotima makes philosophy audible as desire from a position of lack.

crossrefs.note: the philosopher defined by desire for the whole of wisdom

revisions.body: The entrance is heard before it is seen: Alcibiades arrives as a voice from the courtyard, and the fillets held before his eyes prevent him from noticing Socrates as he takes his place beside Agathon. I read that blocked recognition as the scene’s dramatic hinge: the new speaker enters to crown Agathon, yet the gesture temporarily conceals the person who will shape his speech.

Eryximachus restores the evening’s procedure: Alcibiades must take his turn, then direct Socrates. The subject shifts from the scheduled praise of Eros to praise of Socrates in the exchange that follows. The asymmetry matters: Alcibiades proposes the rule that Socrates may interrupt a falsehood; Socrates permits truthful speech and grants that permission. The encomium’s controlling protocol is Alcibiades’s, not Socrates’s.

The Republic offers σωφροσύνη as a general philosophical requirement; here it appears as a particular speaker’s testimony about Socrates. The comparison is useful not because the passages repeat one image, but because it changes the scale of the question—from what philosophy requires to how a person claims to recognize it.

crossrefs.note: temperance among the philosopher’s necessary natural endowments

revisions.title: The close: persistence without assent
revisions.body: The ending separates persistence from assent. The revelers’ arrival breaks the symposium’s order; by dawn Agathon, Aristophanes, and Socrates alone remain awake, with Socrates still conversing. Socrates has pressed the two men toward the unity of comedy and tragedy, but the report says they follow only with difficulty and fall asleep in turn. The scene leaves a live thesis, not a recorded agreement.

The disruption is structural: the revelers fill the room with noise, and drinking proceeds without order. The dawn scene does not prove that the survivors have mastered the night. It records three men still awake—Agathon, Aristophanes, and Socrates—with Socrates conversing; the two men then follow his comedy-and-tragedy thesis only weakly before sleep overtakes them. Hear the contrast as an interpretation: conversation persists, but no one is shown to stand outside the night’s disorder.

The report preserves only the argument’s headline: Socrates presses Agathon and Aristophanes toward the claim that one person can make both comedy and tragedy. Aristodemus does not remember the rest, and the two men follow only with difficulty. What should we make of an ending that withholds the steps of the argument: does the missing middle invite us to treat the thesis as a conclusion, a test, or an unfinished pressure?
